To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) a large-bore dialysis catheter may be inadvertently positioned in an anomalous pulmonary venous connection; (b) high PO2 and low PCO2 values may be seen in such patients; and (c) Computed Tomography is the imaging modality of choice to locate the catheter tip.
a high PO2 in a dialysis catheter is not necessarily a sign of arterial puncture, and that an anomalous pulmonary venous connection may cause this finding.

(a) a high PO2 and low PCO2 in a patient receiving continuous venovenous hemofiltration is not necessarily a sign of arterial catheterization; (b) the catheter tip may be located in a pulmonary vein, rather than in an innominate vein or carotid artery; (c) a CT Angiogram may be required to locate the catheter tip.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and testing of a novel method for the detection of arterial oxygen saturation in the presence of an anomalous pulmonary venous return.
the study of the influence of different types of catheterization on the blood pressure and heart rate in the patients of the intensive care unit of the hospital of the University of Granada (Spain).
the problem of the catheterization of the left internal jugula vein in the patients with the partial anomalous pulmonary veins.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a high PO2 and low PCO2 in the blood gas obtained from a dialysis catheter should raise the possibility of an arterial cannulation, but should not be the only factor to make this diagnosis.
the finding of increased PO2 during hemodialysis catheter cannulation is not a definitive sign of arterial cannulization.

a high PO2 and low PCO2 in the absence of arterial waveforms and a normal pressure tracing, is not a sign of arterial catheterization, and that the catheter tip location should be confirmed by Computed Tomography or Magnetic Resonance Angiography.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the PO2 and PCO2 of blood drawn from a catheter can be helpful in determining whether the catheter tip has been placed into an artery or a vein.
a high PO2 and a low PCO2 are not always indicative of arterial cannulation.
a high PO2 and low PCO2 in the absence of arterial wave form should raise suspicion for a pulmonary vein cannulation, and should be confirmed by chest X-ray and CT angiogram.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a PO2 > 100 mmHg is not always a sign of arterial catheter placement, and that the tip of a dialysis catheter should not be placed in the innominate vein.
the finding of high PO2 during dialysis catheter insertion is a sign of arterialization of the catheter, and should be investigated further with chest X-ray and Computed Tomographic angiography.
a high PO2 and low PCO2 should not be the only parameters to determine the correct location of the dialysis catheter.
